Question ten. How does a convolutional neural network, or CNN, work? It slides small learned filters over the image, each computing a local weighted sum. This three-by-three filter lights up on a handwritten zero's vertical edges. Each output sees a small patch through one shared filter, so a pattern is found anywhere: shift the digit two pixels right, and the map shifts with it. Pooling then shrinks it, tolerating small shifts. Question eleven. Why are CNNs well suited to images compared to a fully-connected net? Count weights. For a color image two hundred and twenty-four pixels square, a dense layer to a thousand units needs a hundred and fifty million; the page's first convolution, four hundred and forty-eight. The page's whole network has five thousand four hundred and eighteen. But its first layer reuses each weight at fifty thousand positions: twenty-two million multiply-adds, cheap to store, not to compute. That built-in assumption, that nearby pixels belong together, is why a CNN needs far less data.

Two quick ones. Transfer learning: start from a pretrained network. With little data, freeze it and train a new head; with more, fine-tune some or all layers. It cuts data and compute, and one frozen backbone can serve many heads. Why pair softmax with cross-entropy? Their combined gradient is prediction minus target, large exactly when the model is confidently wrong. Libraries fuse them on raw logits, so don't apply softmax first: applied twice over ten classes, the right class tops out at twenty-three percent, and the loss can't drop below one point four six. Last, sequences.
